h1:
Kalasin Desserts
Local Sweets, Sticky Rice & Market Treats
intro: Kalasin isn't only about savory Isan food — its sweets have plenty of stories too. From Khao Wong sticky rice, so soft and fragrant it earned GI status, to old-school Thai sweet shops in town, to the brightly colored dinosaur-egg jellies that have become the local souvenir of Thailand's dinosaur city. We've rounded up the local sweets and dessert shops that Kalasin people actually eat and that are open right now, with where to find them, roughly what they cost, and what's worth grabbing in the evening markets.

blocks.html: Isan desserts are built on sticky rice and cane sugar, and Kalasin is no exception — but it has its own standouts, like Khao Wong sticky rice that people across the country seek out, plus a new generation of dessert shops that play with the city's dinosaur theme until they've become the souvenir everyone wants to take home. This article splits things into three groups: traditional local sweets, Thai-sweet and dessert shops you can sit down at or buy from, and snacks along the evening markets — so you can pick easily depending on whether you're after a casual bite or something to bring home.

Before we run through the shops, let's get to know the homestyle sweets you'll find at Kalasin's morning markets and merit-making events. Most are made from sticky rice, coconut, and sugar — ingredients every Isan household has on hand. They're not overly sweet, so they go well with coffee or iced tea.

items.name: Khao Wong sticky rice (GI)
items.blurb: A premium sticky rice from Khao Wong district, grown by the Phu Thai people on volcanic soil. It's prized because it steams up soft and fragrant and stays tender even after it cools. It's registered as a Geographical Indication (GI) product, and many people buy it to take home as a gift.

items.name: Khao Ji (grilled sticky rice)
items.blurb: Sticky rice shaped into balls, brushed with egg or salt, then grilled over charcoal until the surface is browned and fragrant while the inside stays soft. It's a genuine Isan morning snack, and at Talat Rong See market they've reshaped it into dinosaur-shaped khao ji that kids love.

items.name: Khanom Tian & Khao Tom Mat
items.blurb: Banana-leaf-wrapped sweets that go with merit-making. Khao tom mat is sweetened sticky rice with banana or beans, while khanom tian has a soft dough filled with mung bean or coconut. You'll find them at morning markets and during festivals.

items.name: Khanom Babin & Khanom Luk Ba
items.blurb: Flour-and-sugar sweets rolled into balls and fried until the outside is crisp and the inside is chewy, with a fragrant coconut aroma. They're old-fashioned snacks you'll still find at markets and at long-running Thai sweet shops.

items.name: Fermented-rice khanom jeen
items.blurb: It's savory rather than sweet, but Kalasin's fermented-rice khanom jeen (rice noodles) is a piece of local know-how. The noodles are dark, chewy, and a touch sour from fermentation, eaten with curry sauce or chili dip. Locals call it khao pun.

items.name: Khao Pong & Khao Taen
items.blurb: Sticky rice pressed into sheets then toasted or fried until puffy and drizzled with cane syrup — crisp, lightly sweet, and keeps for a long time. They're a snack and a gift made in the villages.

blocks.title: Getting the real Khao Wong sticky rice
blocks.html: Genuine Khao Wong sticky rice will state Khao Wong district as the growing area and usually carries a GI mark or the name of a community enterprise group on the bag. It costs a little more than regular sticky rice, which is normal — if you see an unusually low price, ask about the source first. Buying from a souvenir shop in town or at Talat Rong See market is a safer bet.

blocks.text: 10 Kalasin dessert and Thai-sweet shops that are actually open

blocks.html: This ranking isn't a fixed measure of which shop tastes better, since dessert is down to each person's palate — instead it's ordered by local reputation, how worth a stop each place is, and the variety on the menu. The prices listed are rough ranges that may shift with ingredients and timing, so it's worth calling to check closing days before you go.

items.name: O Kanom Thai
items.blurb: A well-known Thai sweet shop in town that people recognize for its dinosaur-egg jelly — clear jelly and coconut jelly piped into dinosaur-egg molds in pretty colors, plus dinosaur-shaped luk chup that have become the city's signature souvenir. Beyond that there's a full lineup of Thai sweets: thong yip, thong yod, khanom chan, and various topped sticky-rice sweets. They make for a good-looking gift to take home.
items.price: Jelly/luk chup from about ฿20–60 · Thai-sweet sets by quantity

items.name: Khanom Thai Orathai
items.blurb: A long-running Thai sweet shop on the Yang Talat district side, where locals buy for merit-making and celebrations. They make a full set of auspicious Thai sweets — thong yip, thong yod, foi thong, met khanun, and khanom chan — pretty in color and not too sweet. You can order sets in advance, making it a good spot for genuine Thai-sweet gifts.
items.meta: Yang Talat subdistrict, Yang Talat district, Kalasin
items.price: Thai sweets from about ฿20–50 · sets arranged to order

items.name: WaanD Waan Yok Kamlang Dee Kalasin
items.blurb: A modern-style Thai-dessert cafe that younger crowds like, serving easy-to-grab Thai sweets in cups — bua loy, tako, coconut-milk desserts — alongside cold drinks. The shop is decorated for photos, so it's a nice spot to sit and rest or buy to go. It's a fresher-feeling dessert option than the traditional sweet shops.
items.meta: Thung Si Mueang Nuea area, Mueang Kalasin district

items.name: Heng Pang Pua, Kalasin branch
items.blurb: An iced-dessert shop with a Yaowarat (Chinatown) recipe that opened a branch in Kalasin town. The draw is shaved ice topped with syrup and a range of fixings starting at just a few tens of baht — great for cooling off in the afternoon in an Isan town that's hot almost year-round.
items.meta: Across from Advice in Kalasin town · open 12:00–21:00 (closed Wed)

items.name: Thai-sweet stalls at Talat Rong See
items.blurb: Talat Rong See is a former rice mill in the city center converted into a lifestyle mall, with several Thai-sweet and dessert stalls — khanom krok, khanom buang, bua loy, and dinosaur khao ji. You can graze on plenty of things in one place, and the airy setting makes it a good evening stroll.

items.name: Dessert stalls at Kalasin night market
items.blurb: The city's long-running evening market, where dessert stalls sit alongside savory ones — various topped sweetened sticky rice, khanom thuay, fried banana, and shaved ice. Market-friendly prices make it a good place to buy something to eat back at your room after you've finished with the savory food.
items.meta: Night market, Kalasin municipality (evening to night)

items.name: Mae Games sweets
items.blurb: A dessert shop that Kalasin locals pass along on social media, making homestyle Thai sweets and baked goods for retail and for resellers. The strength is freshness — made new daily — so it's good for a casual snack or to bring home without ordering ahead.

items.name: Local fermented-rice khanom jeen (khao pun)
items.blurb: If you want to try something local that's half-savory, half-snack, Kalasin's fresh fermented-rice khanom jeen is found at morning markets and khao pun shops in town. The noodles are chewy and soft, eaten with nam ya pa or chili dip. A big shared spread with several sauces runs a couple hundred baht for a group.
items.meta: Morning markets and khao pun shops in Mueang Kalasin
items.price: Plate from about ฿30–50 · sharing set around ฿100

items.name: Yai Nan souvenir shop
items.blurb: A souvenir shop in town that gathers Khao Wong sticky rice, dried homestyle sweets, khao taen, and Kalasin gifts in one place. It's a good last stop before heading home to grab long-keeping sweets to take along, with options across a range of prices.
items.price: Gifts from about ฿40 up by type

items.name: Dinosaur-egg sweet learning spot, Ban Non Buri
items.blurb: The Ban Non Buri community near the Sirindhorn Museum makes filled sweets shaped like dinosaur eggs as a community product. At certain times they open for visitors to watch and try making them — good for those who like local stories and want a sweet that comes with one. Check with the community ahead of your visit.
items.meta: Ban Non Buri, Sahatsakhan district (near Sirindhorn Museum)

blocks.title: Tips for buying desserts as gifts
blocks.html: Fresh Thai sweets like jelly, luk chup, and sweetened sticky rice don't keep long, so if you're traveling far, go for dry items like Khao Wong sticky rice, khao taen, or khao pong that last several days. As for dinosaur-egg jelly, if you buy it on your travel day, eat it that day or the next morning, and ask the shop whether they can box it with padding, since the patterns are fairly delicate.

If you're in Kalasin in the evening, walking the markets is the most fun way to eat dessert — you get to try a little of many things at gentle prices, and you'll find homestyle items the sit-down shops rarely have. Here's what you'll often spot at the stalls.

items: Various topped sweetened sticky rice — sangkhaya custard, krachik coconut, and bean toppings. Made with local sticky rice, so it's soft and fragrant — a top favorite at the evening markets.
Khanom krok & khanom buang — made fresh at the stall, with a fragrant coconut-milk aroma. Eaten hot, they beat anything you take home.
Fried banana & fried taro — crisp snacks at a few baht a bag, perfect for eating as you walk.
Shaved ice & iced sweets — the Isan town's go-to for cooling off, drizzled with syrup and loaded with fixings.
Dinosaur khao ji at Talat Rong See — traditional grilled sticky rice in a fun shape that fits the dinosaur-city theme. Photo-worthy and edible.

blocks.text: Pick a dessert for the moment

blocks.html: Kalasin desserts suit plenty of moments. Try choosing based on whether you're after a casual bite, hunting for a gift, or want something genuinely local.

items: Gifts to take home — Khao Wong sticky rice, khao taen, and dinosaur luk chup from O Kanom Thai: long-keeping and distinctly local.
Chilling and photos — WaanD Waan Yok Kamlang Dee: Thai sweets in cups with cold drinks in a photogenic setting.
Cooling off in the afternoon — Heng Pang Pua or the iced-dessert stalls at the markets: cold shaved ice at easy prices.
Trying local specialties — fermented-rice khanom jeen, khao ji, and khanom babin at the morning markets and Talat Rong See.
Grazing on lots of things — Talat Rong See or the night market in the evening, where you can sample a little of everything.

faq.a: Khao Wong sticky rice is the most famous — a premium sticky rice from Khao Wong district grown by the Phu Thai people, which steams up soft and fragrant and stays tender even after cooling, earning it GI registration. As for the sweet that's become the city's signature souvenir, that's the dinosaur-egg jelly and dinosaur luk chup from O Kanom Thai.

faq.q: Where can I buy dinosaur-egg jelly and dinosaur luk chup?
faq.a: O Kanom Thai on Somphamit Road in Mueang Kalasin district is the shop people know for its dinosaur-egg jelly and dinosaur-shaped luk chup, with plenty of other Thai sweets to choose from. These fresh items are best eaten the same day or the next morning, and ask the shop to box them with padding since the patterns are fairly delicate.

faq.q: How is Khao Wong sticky rice different from regular sticky rice?
faq.a: Khao Wong sticky rice is grown on volcanic soil around Khao Wong district. It steams up with soft grains and a nice aroma, and even after it sits and cools it stays tender rather than turning hard and clumpy, so it pairs well with desserts and som tam. It costs slightly more than regular sticky rice, which is normal — the genuine product usually states the growing area and a GI mark on the bag.

faq.q: Which market should I go to for a dessert walk?
faq.a: Talat Rong See in the city center is a lifestyle mall with several Thai-sweet and dessert stalls, including dinosaur khao ji — plenty to graze on. The night market is the long-running evening market with sweetened sticky rice, khanom thuay, and iced sweets at more budget-friendly prices. Both are lively from evening into the night.

faq.q: Roughly how much do Kalasin desserts cost?
faq.a: Most market desserts are cheap — sweetened sticky rice and bagged sweets start around ฿15–40, jelly and luk chup from about ฿20–60, and iced sweets from about ฿35. Khao Wong sticky rice and dry gifts are priced by weight and type, so a few hundred baht of souvenirs will get you a good variety.
